original_value: In recent years, many qualitative sociologists, anthropologists, and social theorists have critiqued the use of algorithms and other automated processes involved in data science on both epistemological and political grounds. Yet, it has proven difficult to bring these important insights into the practice of data science itself. We suggest that part of this problem has to do with under-examined or unacknowledged assumptions about the relationship between the two fields—ideas about how data science and its critics can and should relate. Inspired by recent work in Science and Technology Studies on interventions, we attempted to stage an encounter in which practicing data scientists were asked to analyze a corpus of critical social science literature about their work, using tools of textual analysis such as co-word and topic modelling. The idea was to provoke discussion both about the content of these texts and the possible limits of such analyses. In this commentary, we reflect on the planning stages of the experiment and how responses to the exercise, from both data scientists and qualitative social scientists, revealed some of the tensions and interactions between the normative positions of the different fields. We argue for further studies which can help us understand what these interdisciplinary tensions turn on—which do not paper over them but also do not take them as given.

result.paraphrase: In recent years, many qualitative sociologists, anthropologists, and social theorists have criticized the use of algorithms and other automated processes in data science on both epistemological and political grounds. Yet bringing these important insights into data science practice itself has proven difficult. We suggest that part of this difficulty stems from underexamined or unacknowledged assumptions about how the two fields relate—ideas about how data science and its critics can and should interact. Drawing on recent Science and Technology Studies work on interventions, we staged an encounter in which practicing data scientists were asked to analyze a corpus of critical social science literature about their work using textual analysis tools such as co-word analysis and topic modelling. The aim was to spark discussion both about the content of these texts and about the possible limits of such analyses. In this commentary, we reflect on the experiment’s planning stages and on how responses to it, from both data scientists and qualitative social scientists, revealed tensions and interactions between the normative positions of the different fields. We call for further studies that can help us understand what these interdisciplinary tensions hinge on—studies that neither smooth them over nor treat them as fixed.
